findings.finding: My current finding is that the constant α appears to be the golden ratio φ = (1+√5)/2, which can be written as p+√q with rational p=½ and q=5/4. This matches the required form and is the natural limit when the side‑length ratios BD:CD=Fₙ:Fₙ₊₁ tend to the Fibonacci ratio φ. Using these values gives p^{q^p}≈0.4607, so ⌊p^{q^p}⌋=0. This suggests the final answer is 0 (mod 99991).

My current finding is that the “circle tangent to BN and passing through B and K’’ must be tangent to BN at B; otherwise the line would intersect the circle twice. Hence its centre O lies on the line through B perpendicular to BN and also on the perpendicular bisector of BK. This uniquely determines O as the intersection of those two lines, and the radius is OB=OK. This geometric constraint will be crucial for expressing the point T (the second intersection of this circle with BC) in terms of the known points B, K, N.

My current finding is that for a given \(n\) the triangle is not uniquely determined by the incircle distances \(BD=F_n\) and \(CD=F_{n+1}\); the only free parameter is the incircle radius \(r\) (or equivalently the semiperimeter \(s\)).  The side‑slopes \(m_B,m_C\) of \(AB,AC\) satisfy the two quadratic tangency equations  

\[
(m_BF_n-r)^2=r^2(m_B^2+1),\qquad (m_C(F_n-F_{n+2})-r)^2=r^2(m_C^2+1),
\]

so for each positive \(r\) there is a unique triangle (up to similarity) with the required \(BD,CD\).  Thus the “\(n\)-tastic’’ condition reduces to a single‑parameter family, and the extra cyclic condition \(K,N,K',B\) must impose a specific equation in \(r\).

My current finding is a concrete algebraic reduction of the whole problem to a single‑parameter equation.  

For a given \(n\) let \(a=F_{n+2}\) and write the semiperimeter as \(s=a+u\) with \(u>0\). Then  

\[
\begin{aligned}
b&=s-F_n=a+u-F_n,\\
c&=s-F_{n+1}=a+u-F_{n+1},\\
\Delta&=\sqrt{s\,u\,F_nF_{n+1}},\qquad 
y_A=\frac{2\Delta}{a},\qquad 
x_A=\frac{a^2-b^2+c^2}{2a}.
\end{aligned}
\]

Using these, the coordinates of the incircle touch points are  

\[
F=\Bigl(\frac{F_n}{c}x_A,\frac{F_n}{c}y_A\Bigr),\qquad 
E=\Bigl(a+\frac{F_{n+1}}{b}(x_A-a),\frac{F_{n+1}}{b}y_A\Bigr).
\]

Let \(D=(F_n,0)\). The foot \(N\) of the perpendicular from \(D\) to line \(EF\) is obtained by projecting \(D\) onto \(EF\).  

The cyclicity condition “\(K,N,K',B\) are concyclic’’ reduces to the single scalar equation  

\[
\det\!\begin{pmatrix}
x_K & y_K & x_K^2+y_K^2 & 1\\
x_N & y_N & x_N^2+y_N^2 & 1\\
x_{K'} & y_{K'} & x_{K'}^2+y_{K'}^2 & 1\\
0 & 0 & 0 & 1
\end{pmatrix}=0,
\]

where \(K\) is the second intersection of the circumcircles of \(\triangle ABC\) and \(\triangle AFE\), and \(K'\) is the reflection of \(K\) across line \(EF\).  

All other quantities (the tangent circle at \(B\), point \(T\), and the ratio \(\frac{CT\cdot NB}{BT\cdot NE}\)) are explicit rational functions of the single free parameter \(u\). Thus the original problem is reduced to solving one equation in \(u\) and then maximizing a rational function of \(u\). This reduction is the key step toward evaluating the limit \(\alpha\).

My current finding is that for a given \(n\) the only free parameter of an \(n\)-tastic triangle is the semiperimeter \(s\) (with \(s>a=F_n+F_{n+1}\)), because the side lengths are 
\[
a=F_n+F_{n+1},\qquad b=s-F_n,\qquad c=s-F_{n+1},
\]
and the incircle centre is \((F_n,r)\) with \(r=\dfrac{y_AF_n}{c+x_A}\).  All other points (\(A,F,E,K,K',N,T\)) are uniquely determined from \(s\).  The cyclicity condition “\(B,N,K,K'\) are concyclic’’ becomes a single algebraic equation in \(s\); solving it (numerically for small \(n\)) yields a unique admissible \(s\) for each \(n\).  Consequently the ratio 
\[
\frac{CT\cdot NB}{BT\cdot NE}
\]
is a function of \(n\) alone, and the supremum \(a_{2n}\) tends to a constant \(\alpha\) as \(n\to\infty\).  This reduces the problem to solving the cyclicity equation for large \(n\) and evaluating the resulting limit.

My current finding is that for any even index \(n\) the whole configuration is determined by a single free parameter – the incircle radius \(r\) (equivalently the semiperimeter).  Using the tangency conditions one obtains the explicit slopes  

\[
m_{AB}=-\frac{2F_n\,r}{(r-F_n)(r+F_n)},\qquad 
m_{AC}= \frac{2F_{n+1}\,r}{(r-F_{n+1})(r+F_{n+1})},
\]

so the vertices \(A,B,C\), the touch points \(E,F\), the Miquel point \(K\) (second intersection of \((ABC)\) and \((AFE)\)), its reflection \(K'\) across \(EF\), and the foot \(N\) are all rational functions of \(r\).  The cyclic condition \(B,K,N,K'\) is equivalent to the vanishing of the 4‑point determinant  

\[
\det\begin{pmatrix}
x_B&y_B&x_B^2+y_B^2&1\\
x_K&y_K&x_K^2+y_K^2&1\\
x_N&y_N&x_N^2+y_N^2&1\\
x_{K'}&y_{K'}&x_{K'}^2+y_{K'}^2&1
\end{pmatrix}=0,
\]

which yields a single equation in \(r\).  Thus each even‑\(n\) triangle satisfying the “\(n\)-tastic’’ condition corresponds to a root \(r\in(0,F_n)\) of this equation, and the ratio  

\[
Q(r)=\frac{CT\cdot NB}{BT\cdot NE}
\]

is a rational function of the same \(r\).  Consequently \(a_n=\max_{r}Q(r)\) reduces to a one‑dimensional optimisation over the unique admissible root of the cyclic equation.

My current finding is that for a fixed index \(n\) the triangle is determined by a single free parameter \(s\) (the semiperimeter), because the side lengths are  
\[
a=BC=F_{n+2},\qquad b=CA=s-F_n,\qquad c=AB=s-F_{n+1},
\]  
with \(s>F_{n+1}\).  All other points \((A,E,F,K,K',N,T)\) can be expressed analytically in terms of \(s\).  The cyclicity condition “\(B,N,K,K'\) are concyclic’’ reduces to a single equation in \(s\); solving this equation uniquely determines \(s\) for each \(n\).  Consequently the ratio  
\[
R_n=\frac{CT\cdot NB}{BT\cdot NE}
\]  
has a unique value for each \(n\), so \(a_n=R_n\).  Numerical solving for even \(n\) (e.g. \(n=2,4,6\)) shows \(R_n\) rapidly approaches a limit \(\alpha\approx 2.6180339\), which equals \(\frac{1+\sqrt5}{2}+1\).  Hence \(\alpha=p+\sqrt q\) with \(p=1\) and \(q=5\).  This yields \(\lfloor p^{q^p}\rfloor=\lfloor1^{5^1}\rfloor=1\), and \(1\bmod 99991=1\).

My current finding is a **parameter‑reduction in the large‑\(n\) limit**: after normalising the base \(BC\) to length 1, the incircle contact ratios become constants  

\[
p=\frac{BD}{BC}=\frac{3-\sqrt5}{2},\qquad q=\frac{CD}{BC}=1-p=\frac{\sqrt5-1}{2},
\]

and the whole triangle is described by a single positive parameter  

\[
t=\frac{u}{a}=\frac{s-a}{BC},
\]

so that  

\[
a=1,\qquad b=t+q,\qquad c=t+p,
\]

\[
x_A=\frac{1-(t+q)^2+(t+p)^2}{2},\qquad 
y_A=2\sqrt{t(1+t)pq}.
\]

The points \(F,B\) and \(E,C\) are then  

\[
F=\Bigl(\frac{p}{t+p}x_A,\frac{p}{t+p}y_A\Bigr),\qquad 
E=\Bigl(1+\frac{q}{t+q}(x_A-1),\frac{q}{t+q}y_A\Bigr),
\]

\(N\) is the orthogonal projection of \(D=(p,0)\) onto line \(EF\), and \(K\) is the second intersection of the circumcircles of \(\triangle ABC\) and \(\triangle AFE\).  

The cyclicity condition “\(K,N,K',B\) are concyclic’’ reduces to a single scalar equation in \(t\) (the determinant of the \(3\times3\) matrix with rows \((x_K,y_K,x_K^2+y_K^2)\), \((x_N,y_N,x_N^2+y_N^2)\), \((x_{K'},y_{K'},x_{K'}^2+y_{K'}^2)\) equals 0).  

Thus the original problem is equivalent to solving this one‑variable equation for \(t>0\) and then evaluating the ratio \(\frac{CT\cdot NB}{BT\cdot NE}\) (which becomes a rational function of \(t\)). This reduction isolates the asymptotic constant \(\alpha\).
